name: Nurses' Station
narrativeOnEnter: A long medical counter runs the length of the room. Medicine cabinets line the wall behind it — most empty, some sealed. An old computer terminal sits in the corner, its amber screen still glowing faintly.

action.text:
A laminated reference card — yellowed but legible.

RECORDS VAULT — SYMBOL REFERENCE GUIDE
(For authorised staff only)

Patient intake symbols are filed in order:
Cross · Moon · Star · Eye

Match the symbols in that sequence on the vault cabinet to release the director's key.

A stack of patient charts. Most are redacted or water-damaged.

One legible entry reads:
'Patient 07 — behavioural changes noted following first treatment session. Patient remains agitated. Requesting review of Director Harlan's protocols.'

But someone has annotated this entry in a different pen:
'Treatment sessions are listed as ECT in the official chart.
But I was on duty for three of them. There was no ECT equipment in that room.
There was a machine I didn't recognise — medical-looking, but not standard.
The sessions lasted 90 minutes. ECT takes 10–20.
I asked Dr. Harlan. He told me it was an "advanced therapeutic protocol." He would not say more.

I cross-referenced the session dates with the maintenance log:
every session, external equipment was brought in via the service entrance.
The delivery company: Δ Medical Dynamics — a subsidiary I looked up.
Parent company: AXIOM Group.

I don't know what they were doing to her.
I'm requesting a formal review and I'm keeping a copy of this note.
— A. Colm, RN'

Nursing staff password for terminal system: BLACKWOOD

A long counter. Scattered across it: empty medication trays, a broken thermometer, a pen.

Something is carved into the countertop — a long message, made with a scalpel tip, carefully:

'If you're reading this, find the vault.
Director Harlan's year of opening = safe code.
Blackwood opened: 1972.

The vault has the proof. AXIOM. Project HELIOS.
They called it a neural mapping study.
They ran it on involuntary patients.
47 of them. All in Ward B.

I submitted my formal objection to Dr. Harlan in October.
He destroyed it.
I submitted it again in November.
He sent me on mandatory leave.

I came back the night Patient 07 left.
Harlan asked me why I was there.
I said: I wanted to make sure she got out safely.
He didn't stop me.
I think he was relieved.

I helped her.
I showed her the tunnel.
I told her: take the list and go.
She took it.
She ran.

I'm not sorry.
— Agnes Colm, Ward B Nurse, 14 November 1972'
